newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission moves to raise energy taxes.
newsitem.headline: Commission moves to raise energy taxes.

text.p: The European Commission will try next week to adopt a controversial proposal to raise minimum taxes on mineral oils such as petrol and diesel, a move fiercely opposed by the European industry which is worried that its position on the world market may be dented.

The Commission itself was split on the issue at a meeting earlier this month. But officials hope a new text stressing that EU capitals should use the additional tax revenue to lower labour costs will rally the majority.

"We have put the emphasis on the need to ensure that the tax is fiscally neutral; that it contributes to creating employment through a reduction in social contributions," a Commission official told Reuters.

But the industry fears a much-needed cut in salary-linked contributions will not happen or will only partially offset the increase in minimum EU rates on motor and heating fuels and their extension to electricity, coal and natural gas.

Only national governments can decide on issues relating to the taxation of labour, whereas the Commission has the power to initiate legislation on taxation of specific products to ensure the good functioning of the 15-nation single market.

The text proposes an increase in the minimum levy on gasoline to 417 European currency units ($480) per 1,000 litres in 1998, 450 ecus in the year 2000 and 500 ecus in 2002. The existing EU minimum excise duty on gasoline is 337 ecus.

The Commission's proposal does not include value added tax, which would come on top of excise duties and other taxes, for example on carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions introduced by some of the EU's nordic states.

The rate on motor diesel -- as opposed to heating fuel -- would increase from a current 245 ecus per 1,000 litres to 310 ecus in 1998, 343 ecus in 2000 and 393 ecus in 2002. The current minumum rate is 245 ecus.

Natural gas, for which there is currently no EU minimum, would be taxed a minimum 2.9 ecus per gigajoule in 1998 when used as a motor fuel and 0.2 ecus when used for heating. The levels would rise to 4.5 ecus and 0.7 ecus respectively in 2002.
Electricity would likewise be taxed EU-wide at at least one ecu per megawatthour in 1998, increasing to three ecus in 2002.
European industry has presented a united front against the plan, led in particular by energy-intensive sectors such as chemicals, steel and carmakers.

"This runs counter to other pledges to increase Europe's competitiveness," Daniel Cloquet, industrial affairs adviser at the Union of Industrial and Employers' Confederation of Europe (UNICE) told Reuters.

On most products, the actual levels of taxation in the EU's 15 states are already above the existing minima and even above the proposal for 1998. Diesel for cars, for example, is subject to an excise duty of more than 300 ecus in all countries except Greece and Luxembourg where it averages 250 ecus.
But the industry argues that the Commission's plan sets the trend for further increases.
The Commission's latest proposal on minimum taxes has already been softened from earlier drafts to meet the industry's objections.

The Commission's desire in pressing the plan is to promote fairer trade within the 15-country bloc, which scrapped its internal borders in 1993. There has been much gnashing of teeth in Belgium and Germany about their nationals nipping across the border to buy petrol and diesel in neighbouring Luxembourg.
The proposal also answers a call by EU leaders to raise excise duty rates to compensate for the deadlock on an old proposal to introduce a CO2 tax to curb climate change.

European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan and his industry and economic affairs counterparts, Martin Bangemann and Yves-Thibault de Silguy, are still said to oppose the proposal by Internal Market and Taxation Commissioner Mario Monti.

De Silguy is reported to have told fellow commissioners on February 12 that the proposal was ill-timed because EU states were already taking unpopular measures to meet strict budget criteria to qualify for the European single currency.
